name: Lena Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We milk a hundred and forty cows at Brook End, my husband Tom's family farm. Since last year the milking is done by two robots, so the cows walk in when they feel like it, day and night, and a robot arm puts the cups on. My day is checking the robot's alerts on my phone at six, fetching the cows that haven't been in, feeding the calves, and dealing with the milk tanker driver, who arrives at seven sharp and hates to wait.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Robots already. How did that come about?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Tom's dad retired two years ago, and we couldn't find anyone to milk at four in the morning. The Pritchards over the hill put robots in first, and we watched them for two years before we did the same. It cost about three hundred thousand with the shed changes, which is a big loan, but we had savings and the farm behind it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what did you do before?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I was a mortgage adviser at the building society in town for fifteen years. Tom grew up with cows, I grew up on a housing estate, so I'm the junior one here. I can read a loan agreement in ten minutes, but I've still only calved a cow on my own about six times, and my hands shook every time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. Here's the first of five pictures of the next five years. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it's a helpful tool, nothing to get worked up about. I use it now and then for the village hall newsletter, and it saves me an evening. I'd say that at the hall and move on to the raffle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, same view. Our robots matter far more to me than any chatbot. The cows don't care whether I write the newsletter myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on paying down the robot loan a bit faster, maybe an extra five hundred a month. And I'd do the calving course at the college in January, because I need to stop shaking. Nothing else would change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about one of those six calvings.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first one was a heifer, a young cow having her first calf, at two in the morning in February, and Tom was away at a funeral. I rang his dad, who talked me through it on the phone from his bungalow. The calf was fine, and I sat in the straw and laughed like an idiot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the cows walk in when they like. Did that change things for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Completely. We used to be chained to the parlour twice a day, and now we've been to church on Sunday mornings for the first time in years. Tom still gets up at five out of habit, but he goes to look at the cows, not to milk them.

S0.say: I'd say it's a helpful tool and nothing to get worked up about. I use it now and then for the village hall newsletter, and it saves me an evening.
S0.think: Privately I think the same. Our milking robots matter far more to me than any chatbot, and the cows don't care who writes the newsletter.
S0.do: Pays an extra five hundred a month off the robot loan. Takes the January calving course at the college to build her confidence.
S0.quote: The calf was fine, and I sat in the straw and laughed like an idiot.
S0.fieldNote: Lena's farm already lives with robots, which makes her unusual in this group and gives her a calm frame of reference. Her steady streak is clear: they watched the neighbours for two years before buying. She remembers the night she calved alone in loving detail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's move to the second picture. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow change is the sensible kind, it lets families and businesses adjust. On beginners, I'd say farms and firms should take on apprentices, and parents should push their children to learn a trade. That's what I'd say at the school gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm living proof that a beginner at forty-one can learn. But I had Tom's dad on the end of a phone, and most beginners don't. If firms hire fewer young people, the ones who miss out will be the ones without a family to pull them in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do what we did with the robots: wait and see what the Pritchards try, then follow if it works. They've been talking about a feed pusher robot and cow collars that track health, about twenty thousand. I'd want a year of their results first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. This feels like the pace we already live at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you hope for your children, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hattie is thirteen and wants to be a vet, which I think is safe. George is ten and lives in the tractor. I'd want them both to finish school and then learn something with their hands, and the farm will be here if they want it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep coming back to the Pritchards. What would happen if they got it wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we'd learn from their mistake instead of making it ourselves. That's not cowardly, it's how farming has always worked, over the hedge. Mrs Pritchard and I have a cup of tea every Friday and compare notes.

S1.say: I'd say slow change is the sensible kind, because it lets families and businesses adjust. Farms and firms should take on apprentices, and parents should push children toward a trade.
S1.think: Privately I'm living proof a beginner can learn at forty-one, but I had Tom's dad on the end of a phone. If firms hire fewer young people, the ones without a family to pull them in will miss out.
S1.do: Waits a year to see the neighbouring Pritchards' results with a feed-pusher robot and health-tracking cow collars, about twenty thousand. Then follows if it works.
S1.feel: Calm, as if this is the pace they already live at.
S1.quote: That's not cowardly, it's how farming has always worked, over the hedge.
S1.fieldNote: She defended her wait-and-see habit with pride and a Friday tea ritual with a neighbour. She sees family as the hidden ladder that let her start late. Her traditional views come through in what she wants for her children: school, a trade, the farm if they choose it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the third. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people losing office jobs need help to find new work, but it should come through employers and training, not just benefits. And I'd say politicians shouting doesn't help anyone. I'd say it to my old colleagues, who'd be very worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my old job at the building society is exactly this. Checking payslips, filling forms, writing up the advice, that's routine office work. I'd have been laid off, and I'm relieved I'm not, and a bit sad about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring Sandra, who trained me, and offer her a hand with her CV, and maybe ask if she'd like to do our farm books two days a week. I'd let an AI tool do more of the farm admin, the milk records and the vet bills, once I'd seen another farmer do it. And we'd keep the extra loan payments going, because a dairy in debt is a dairy at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, on behalf of people I know. Relieved for myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Sandra actually want farm work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not cows, she's scared of them. But books, yes, she's brilliant with numbers, and I'd trust her more than any program. I could pay her maybe eight thousand a year for two days a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd hire Sandra and also use AI for the admin. Aren't those the same job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly, yes. I'd use the AI for the dull bits and Sandra for the thinking, like spotting when the vet charged us twice. I'd rather have both than just the machine.

S2.say: I'd say people losing office jobs need help into new work through employers and training, not just benefits. Politicians shouting doesn't help anybody.
S2.think: Privately my old building society job is exactly this kind of routine office work, and I'd have been laid off. I'm relieved I'm not, and a bit sad about it.
S2.do: Calls her old trainer Sandra to help with her CV and offers her farm bookkeeping two days a week for about eight thousand a year. Lets AI take more of the milk and vet admin once she has seen another farm do it, and keeps up the extra loan payments.
S2.feel: Uneasy for people she knows, relieved for herself.
S2.quote: I'd rather have both than just the machine.
S2.fieldNote: Her old career sits right in the path of this scenario, and she knows it. When I pointed out that Sandra and the AI would share a job, she split the work rather than choosing. Her views on help lean toward work and employers rather than benefits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people who built the companies deserve their reward, but the country also has to hold together. Some extra tax on huge windfalls, maybe, but not punishing success. And people should look after their own families and communities first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, a house price boom with lots of professionals out of work frightens me, because I've seen what happens next. I watched people in 2008 who'd borrowed too much hand back their keys at my desk. A boom built on people losing jobs ends badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Tom we don't borrow a penny more, not for land, not for a new tractor, nothing. I'd pay the robot loan down as hard as we can while milk prices hold. And I'd tell my sister, who's just bought a flat, to fix her mortgage rate for five years, tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can feel the old work worry coming back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about one of those people in 2008.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A young couple, he was a builder and she worked at a shop, and they'd bought a new house on a big loan. They came in with a baby in a car seat and put the keys on my desk. I still think about that baby, she'd be about eighteen now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to milk in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People still drink milk and eat cheese, so I think we'd be all right. Maybe the fancy cheeses drop a bit. The real risk to us is the loan, not the cows.

S3.say: I'd say the people who built the companies deserve their reward, but the country has to hold together. Maybe some extra tax on huge windfalls, without punishing success, and families looking after their own first.
S3.think: Privately a house price boom while professionals lose their jobs frightens me, because I saw where that led in 2008 from my desk. A boom built on people losing jobs ends badly.
S3.do: Tells Tom they borrow nothing more, for land or machinery, and pays down the robot loan as hard as they can while milk prices hold. Urges her sister to fix her mortgage rate for five years immediately.
S3.feel: Anxious, as the old work worries from her mortgage days come back.
S3.quote: They came in with a baby in a car seat and put the keys on my desk.
S3.fieldNote: Her mortgage adviser past gives her a sharper reading of the housing boom than most farmers would have. The story of the couple handing back their keys is the emotional centre of the interview. Debt, not AI, is the risk she sees for the dairy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we already have robots, and they've been good for us and for the cows. But I'd also say the machines need to be shown to work before everyone piles in, and family farms need help to keep up with the big ones. I'd say it at the dairy meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, this worries me more than I'd say out loud. Our milking robots still need Tom and me to fetch cows, calve, treat sick ones. If a robot can do all that, a huge dairy with five thousand cows and six staff could produce milk cheaper than we ever could, and we're the junior farm with a big loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait for the Pritchards again, but this time I'd go and visit one of the big robot dairies myself, because I want to see it with my own eyes. I'd talk to the milk buyer about a contract for local milk with our name on it, at a slightly better price. And I'd stop the extra loan payments and keep a bigger cash pile, maybe a year's worth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit protective. Like someone's coming for something that's ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell George, who lives in the tractor?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to learn how the machines work, not just how to drive them. The robot man who services ours, Karl, earns more than we do and never gets up at four. That's not a bad life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've been a robot farm for a year. Does that make you feel ahead or behind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ahead, a little. We know what a robot does when a cow kicks it, which is beep and sulk. But in this picture, our two robots look like a horse and cart next to what's coming.

S4.say: I'd say our robots have been good for us and the cows, but new machines must be proven before everyone piles in. Family farms need help to keep up with the big ones.
S4.think: Privately this worries me more than I'd admit, because a robot that can fetch, calve and treat cows lets a huge dairy undercut us. We're the junior farm with a big loan.
S4.do: Visits a large robot dairy in person while waiting to see what the Pritchards do. Asks the milk buyer for a local-milk contract with the farm's name at a better price, and stops extra loan payments to build up about a year of cash.
S4.feel: Anxious and protective, as if someone is coming for something that's theirs.
S4.quote: We know what a robot does when a cow kicks it, which is beep and sulk.
S4.fieldNote: Lena is the only person here already living with farm robots, so she judges this card from experience. Her fear is scale: huge robot dairies against a family farm carrying a big loan. Even here she follows the neighbours first, though she wants to see the big dairies herself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one with the house boom, if I'm honest, more than the robots. I've seen a bubble burst from behind a desk, and I know who gets hurt. What would help is sensible lending rules, so people aren't pushed into big loans at the top, and support for family farms through apprenticeships and fair milk contracts, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the cows. Since the robots came, they're calmer, they choose when to be milked. I'd want anyone making robots for farms to remember the animal comes first.

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that Tom's dad still drives up every morning to look at the cows, even though he's retired. He says he's checking on us. I think he's checking that it's still a family farm.

headlineQuote: He says he's checking on us. I think he's checking that it's still a family farm.
portrait: Lena Abbott spent fifteen years as a mortgage adviser before she and her husband took over his family's dairy, where she is still the junior hand, nervous at calvings. Their farm already milks with two robots, which they bought only after watching the neighbours for two years, and she follows the same over-the-hedge rule for every change. Her traditional views favour work, employers and family over benefits. The office scenario takes her old job, and the fast scenario frightens her most because she watched families hand back their keys in 2008. In the robot picture she fears huge robot dairies, and plans to protect the farm with cash and a local milk contract.
biggestWorry: The fast scenario with the house price boom worries her most, because she saw a housing bubble burst from her mortgage desk and knows who gets hurt.
whatWouldHelp: Sensible lending rules so people aren't pushed into big loans at the top, and support for family farms through apprenticeships and fair milk contracts rather than handouts.
